articles.title: A Crash at Item 27 Should Not Cost You 27 Calls
articles.excerpt: My digest worker died at 2:14 a.m. on item 27 of 40. The traceback was a timeout — unremarkable, the kind of thing a free endpoint does on a slow night. I restarted the script and watched it summarize…
articles.body: My digest worker died at 2:14 a.m. on item 27 of 40. The traceback was a timeout — unremarkable, the kind of thing a free endpoint does on a slow night. I restarted the script and watched it summarize items 1 through 26 all over again. Those summaries were already on disk, already correct, already paid for in tokens. I paid twice for the same twenty-six paragraphs because my script had no memory of ever having done them. So here is the question I actually care about: can you make a batch worker that resumes instead of restarting, in a way that makes a flaky free tier boring? Yes — and the whole mechanism is one table with one column that decides whether a request is new or already answered.

articles.title: Cancelled Is a Terminal State, Not an Exception
articles.excerpt: A support ticket landed on a Tuesday: a user closed the tab forty seconds into a long summary, reopened the app, and found two generations billed against her workspace. Nothing in the logs was red. Th…
articles.body: A support ticket landed on a Tuesday: a user closed the tab forty seconds into a long summary, reopened the app, and found two generations billed against her workspace. Nothing in the logs was red. The job row said running , the ledger said charged , and the provider dashboard said the call had finished normally — because from the provider's point of view, nobody ever hung up. That ticket is the whole article. We keep treating "cancel" as a piece of UI candy: a stop button that flips local state and lets the expensive part keep going. I think that is backwards. Cancellation is a distributed transaction, and it only counts when it reaches every party that can spend your money — the model provider, your persistence layer, and whoever reads the ledger afterward.
articles.author: kongkong

articles.title: Before You Move a Workload to the Free AI Lane, Run the Flip Test
articles.excerpt: The question landed at minute forty of a planning call: "why don't we just put everything on the free lane and revisit next quarter?" It is a fair question, and it is usually answered badly — with a p…
articles.body: The question landed at minute forty of a planning call: "why don't we just put everything on the free lane and revisit next quarter?" It is a fair question, and it is usually answered badly — with a price comparison, or with a vibe about model quality. Both miss the thing that actually decides the outcome. The scene is a composite, assembled from conversations I keep having with platform leads. No client numbers below, and no measured benchmarks. The lane you pick is a statement about what you can refuse There are three lanes most teams are actually choosing between: Hosted free allowance — zero contract, zero ops, shared infrastructure, terms you don't control. Hosted paid — a contract, per-unit billing, stronger retention and version guarantees.

articles.title: The file that governs 132 pages is imported by seven of them, and one page claims what it refuses to
articles.excerpt: CogniPrep has 132 employer guide pages: cogniprep.app/employers lists every one of them, and each answers "what assessment will I sit if I apply here". Pages like that are easy to write badly. The tem…
articles.body: CogniPrep has 132 employer guide pages: cogniprep.app/employers lists every one of them, and each answers "what assessment will I sit if I apply here". Pages like that are easy to write badly. The temptation is to reason from the sector, notice that three banks in a peer group use the same vendor, and write the fourth page as if it did too. So the associations live in one file with a rule at the top: 1. Every association carries a URL someone actually opened. No URL, no entry. 2. No association is inferred from sector norms or from what peers use. An employer with no evidence gets an empty `associations` array, and the site says so rather than guessing. That file is now 239,378 bytes and 4,915 lines, and it holds 239 employer profiles carrying 263 citations.

articles.body: NASA is overhauling how it selects and develops science missions, with changes intended to reduce costs, streamline competition and get missions into space faster. The new approach, called Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), was announced on Oct. 21 in an open letter from Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate (SMD), to the NASA science community. The changes, directed by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, could significantly reshape how scientists, universities, NASA centers and commercial companies vie for future missions. "We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long," Fox stated in the letter.

articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.body: The October full moon rises tonight! Here's everything you need to know about the "Hunter's Moon," including where to see it, how it got its name and other tricks of the light and mind that could conspire to create a truly spectacular lunar light show. October's moon reaches 100% illumination at 12:12 a.m. EDT (0412 GMT) on Oct. 26, as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. The shadowy terminator that separates the day and night side of the moon is conspicuously absent around this time, as are the shadows that throw craters into spectacular relief during the waxing and waning lunar phases.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
